Nevertheless, global prospects are improving. Wood Mackenzie forecasts global industrial production growth to accelerate to 3.5% in 2013, up from 2.85 in 2012. 

It is safe to say that the world’s improving prospects are centred in the emerging economies. Latest data suggests that China’s economy is accelerating through the end of 2012. Manufacturing indicators have improved, and an upturn in China’s construction industry should support more robust growth through 2013. But the rebalancing of China’s economy away from investment towards consumption means the positive outlook for parts of Chinese industry is far from certain. Growth in other emerging economies such as Brazil and India should also accelerate next year, supported by more favourable government policies. The sustainability of such growth, however, remains a question. 

The industrial outlook for the developed economies is not as rosy. After a slow start to next year, we do expect to see a gradual improvement in developed world growth as we head towards 2014. But uncertainty around the US fiscal position is a key risk, while further austerity measures across Europe will continue to drag on growth, threatening the stability of the Eurozone. 

### **Global growth in industry to be driven by non-OECD economies** 



## **USA** 

US industrial production has been flat in 2012, losing momentum from the robust growth of 2011. Output in October was identical to that of January. A critical reason for the lack of industrial growth in 2012 has been business investment. Through much of 2011, firms invested heavily in capital goods (equipment and software in particular) to take advantage of tax breaks and make their processes more efficient.  This assisted recovery in durable goods production but has since fallen away as a driver of industrial production.  Business investment is hampered by an uncertain outlook, and concerns about the looming fiscal cliff appear to be deterring activity. The latest leading indicators (specifically the new orders component of the manufacturing purchasing managers’ indices) show manufacturing order books shrinking towards year end, suggesting that further weakness in industrial output should be expected in early 2013.Industrial output for 2012 as a whole should record growth of around 3.6%, reflecting the low base of early 2011. However, due to the lack of industrial growth drivers, we expect to see growth slow to just 1.7% in 2013. 

We have made no changes to our medium- to long-term outlook for US industrial production since our last update, but there is potential upside stemming from developments in the energy sector. US gas and oil production is expanding, resulting in extremely low natural gas prices. Consequently, some energy intensive industries, such as petrochemicals and DRI (steel)

, are likely to expand production as we look into the medium-term (2016 and beyond). While the direct impact of these industries may not be that large, the knock-on effects on related industries may be beneficial to total industrial production growth, especially in the latter half of this decade.

## **Japan** 

Japan experienced a rebound in industrial production in early 2012, as output recovered from supply-chain disruptions following the flooding in Thailand in late 2011. But as 2012 has progressed, there has been a steady deterioration in industrial activity; output contracted by 7.5% between April and October. Industrial activity began to trend lower due to a combination of weak exports and the expiration of domestic incentive schemes. Exports of electronic goods in particular suffered, as the recession in Europe took its toll on demand. The recent territorial dispute with China has worsened the situation, as many Chinese firms have substituted imports from Japan for those from South Korea and Taiwan. While it is unclear how events will play out between China and Japan, it seems safe to say that there will not be a switch back to Japanese goods any time soon. Lead indicators remain depressed, reinforcing our view that Japanese industrial activity at best grow weakly in 2013. Wood Mackenzie forecasts zero growth in IP in 2012, and just 1.2% in 2013. This would leave the level of activity 13% shy of its 2007 peak. 

Recent developments do offer some potential upside for Japanese industry. The strength of the yen has been a huge burden on Japanese exporters in the past few years, eroding their export competitiveness. At the time of writing, Japan was a few days away from going to the polls for parliamentary elections, and it is expected that the Liberal Democratic Party, led by Shinzo Abe, will return to power. Much of Mr Abe’s campaign has focussed on raising Japan’s inflation target to at least 2%. For a country where inflation has average -0.3% over 20 years, this would be a major change and require massive monetary stimulus. Such a move would place significant downward pressure on the yen – a welcome respite for Japan’s struggling exporters. 

Our view on Japanese growth over the long-term remains unchanged but downside risks remain. The steady decline in Japan’s working age population (which began in 1997 and is gathering momentum) is a key factor pushing Japan’s overall IP growth down to 1% per annum by 2020.  Japan’s high value-add manufacturing has been under threat for some time from growth in high-tech industrial economies such as South Korea and Singapore, where costs are lower and an increasingly skilled labour force available. But the decision to phase out nuclear power generation in the coming decades may push up power costs for Japanese industry, providing further incent

ive for firms to reassess their investment plans and step up the pace of industrial off-shoring. 

## **Europe** 

Industrial activity continues to contract across Europe. While the contractions are most acute in the periphery, even economies such as Germany, the Netherlands and France are experiencing falling industrial production. As a result, activity for the EU 27 as a whole fell by 1.7% year on year through the first three quarters of 2012. There is little hope for a sharp rebound in growth anytime soon – Europe’s economies will continue to be weighed down by austere government policies and uncompetitive industries. Wood Mackenzie’s latest forecast expects IP in the EU to shrink by 1.8% in 2012 and to see zero growth in 2013. 

The extent of the contraction in industry across some European economies is massive. The level of activity in Spain and Italy is 29% and 25% below the respective pre-crisis peaks, and continues to fall. We have serious concerns that much of this contraction will be permanent, that capacity has been destroyed. This seems especially likely in Spain, where much of the pre-crisis growth in industry was driven by a housing bubble that burst in spectacular fashion. Given that the

fall in capacity utilisation is significantly less than that of industry in both countries, it would seem that numerous firms have gone out of business or scaled back operations. The implication is that even if the reforms being pushed through economies can improve labour market efficiency, even when Economic growth across Europe resumes, industry cannot recover to the pre-crisis level of output without investing in new industrial capacity. It is highly questionable whether the Eurozone’s peripheral economies are an attractive investment destination, given the uncertainty around the single currency and sovereign debt positions. 

Europe’s core economies have for the most part outperformed their southern counterparts; economies such as Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands were close to pre-crisis levels of industrial production by the end of 2011. But even industry in these economies has been unable to shrug off the recession of 2012 across Europe. Activity has been falling through much of the year, and the level of activity in Germany in October was down 3.6% from a year earlier. With European economic growth in 2013 likely to be extremely weak once again, we do not expect to see much of a pick-up in industry in the core economies. We forecast German IP to fall by 0.8% in 2012, and be flat in 2013. France, Belgium and the Netherlands are expected to see further contractions in IP in 2013. On the plus side, there is little to suggest that these core countries have suffered any permanent loss in production. When demand begins to pick up we would expect them to fully recover. France and the UK might be the exceptions however –utilisation data suggests that

they may have suffered some loss of capacity. 

Among Europe’s best performing nations are those of the east, although growth has slowed in comparison to pre-crisis years. Polish industrial production was 11% above the previous peak in January 2008. Poland’s IP was buoyed by spillover effects from infrastructure construction associated with hosting the UEFA Football Championships in the summer of 2012. But, the external environment is taking its toll with IP growth stagnating so far this year. IP in October was up by just 0.6% year on year. We expect Polish industrial output growth to remain modest in 2013 at 2.3%, down from 2.4% in 2012, due to ongoing export weakness. 

Wood Mackenzie’s medium term outlook for European industrial output is modest. Although the sense of crisis has mostly passed from the Eurozone, there is no quick fix for peripheral economies. Consolidating sovereign debt and improving competitiveness will take time – probably as much as a decade. Protracted restructuring in Europe will weigh on economic growth and industrial production well out into the medium term outlook. 

Europe’s long term growth prospects are unchanged from the previous update. We do expect to see some improvement in Spain and Italy, supported by reduced labour costs and deregulation in industry, but Western European countries as a whole will be constrained by significant demographic factors – ageing populations and in some instances a shrinking working age population. Germany and Italy alone will see their working age populations shrink by around a total of 11 million people over the next two decades (3m in Italy and 8m in Germany). In order to maintain output at close to current levels, labour force participation rates and productivity will need to increase to offset this demographic change. In eastern European economies, growth will be higher since the potential for productivity gains are greater and they will transition to higher value added industries through time. We forecast EU industrial production growth to average 1.2% from 2013 – 2030.

## **China** 

It is becoming increasingly apparent that China’s economy has turned a corner, and that industrial growth is accelerating. Industrial production growth slowed from 12.8% year on year in December 2011 to a low of 8.9% in August, on the back of weak export growth, especially to Europe, and a slowdown in domestic construction activity. The slowdown in real estate was deliberately engineered by the government in previous years to prevent overly-rapid rises in house prices, but arguably we underestimated the knock-on effects the slowdown in construction would have on other industries such as machinery, white goods and raw materials. 

While export growth will remain relatively muted in the near term, construction activity is increasi

ng. House prices started to reverse their decline during the third quarter, prompting increasing sales and construction volumes. Property sales growth accelerated to 30% year on year in November and apparent demand for finished steel (a useful proxy for construction volumes) climbed to 18% year on year in October.  This is feeding through into industrial production, with growth climbing back above 10% year on year in November. The manufacturing PMI also rose to its highest level since May 2011, giving a good indication that manufacturing will see further gains in the coming months. Wood Mackenzie forecasts IP growth to accelerate to 10.7% in 2013, up from 9.9% in 2012. 

China’s long-term IP growth forecast is unchanged since our last update, but there is increased uncertainty around the view. We continue to forecast a very gradual decline in industrial growth this decade, based on the assumption that China can leverage off its increasingly skilled workforce and extensive manufacturing infrastructure to move up the manufacturing value chain. But the rebalancing of China’s economy away from exports and investment towards consumption will challenge the parts of industry that are very much geared towards Chinese investment. Wood Mackenzie forecasts Chinese industrial production growth to drop below 10% per annum by 2020, reaching 6.4% in 2030. 

### **Industrial production growth in major developing economies (year on year)** 



## **India** 

India’s industrial sector has performed poorly throughout 2012, growing just 0.3% year on year through the first threequarters, as tight monetary policy and a lack of investment has hampered activity. Capital goods production in particular has been weak through 2012; capital goods demand is tied to investment growth, which has been deterred by high interest rates and bureaucratic obstacles. Wood Mackenzie expects IP growth of just 1.3% in 2012. 

There have been some potentially encouraging signs in the past few months that give hope of faster growth in 2013. In October, industrial production recorded annual growth of 8.2%, a sharp improvement from the -0.7% in September. But a large part of the increase is likely due to base effects; the Hindu festival of Diwali took place in October last year but November in 2012. Nevertheless, there does appear to be some upward momentum in the data in recent months. In addition, investment activity may receive a boost from the recent economic reform measures announced by the government. But this would likely be sentiment driven – even if the reforms are implemented they will take at least a year to filter through into real growth. Wood Mackenzie forecasts industrial production growth to accelerate to 4.6% in 2013 and 6.1% in 2014.

## **Brazil** 

After a torrid 18 months, industrial activity in Brazil is showing some signs of improvement. Growth slowed to 0.3% in 2011, from 10.

6% the previous year, and the weakness carried through into early 2012. Manufacturing activity was weighed down by high labour costs, a strong currency, falling investment and a sharp contraction in Brazil’s auto industry. In an attempt to reinvigorate Brazil’s faltering industry, the government introduced a raft of measures to boost manufacturing competiveness, and interest rates have been slashed. Payroll taxes have been cut in an attempt to ease labour costs, electricity tariffs for industry have fallen, and infrastructure bottlenecks are being addressed. In addition, there has been a boom in auto production, which makes up 20% of Brazilian manufacturing, following vehicle sales tax breaks. The result has been a return to industrial growth, with positive annual growth in October for the first time since August 2011. We expect to see Brazilian industry make further gains in the short term – the manufacturing PMI is currently at a 20-month high. However, there are some doubts around the sustainability of growth once government stimulus measures expire. Wood Mackenzie forecasts IP growth to bounce back in 2013 to 3.5%, up from -2.1% in 2012. There is no change to Brazil’s medium- to long-term growth prospects. Brazil’s industrial production growth potential is robust but remains contingent on the effectiveness of policies to promote productivity growth and provide employment for a growing working age-population. Large-scale investment in infrastructure will also be essential for the economy to realise its potential. This would mean the second fastest year of growth (behind 2010) since 1980. Like 2010, the primary reason for such rapid growth is recovery from a bad previous year. In 2011, natural disasters in Japan and Thailand caused global disruptions to vehicle production, while demand in China, the world’s largest market, was stagnant. In 2012, supply disruptions have been minimal and inventories restocked, while China has resumed modest growth. In addition, the US has posted double-digit growth for the third straight year. The prospects for 2013 are not as strong, and we forecast global production growth slow to 3.6%. Although we expect to see improving vehicle demand and production growth in emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil, this will be offset by slower growth in the US and contraction in Europe and Japan. In some respects, 2013 sets the tone for the medium to longer term view; global vehicle production growth will continue to be driven by emerging markets, especially in Asia. Over 50% of incremental vehicle production between 2010 and 2030 will be take place in Asia, with China and India accounting for the lion’s share. ### **Global auto production – growth accelerates** ## **Japan** 2012 has been all about recovery for Japan’s auto industry, with output at its highest since before the financial crisis. But the improvements of 2012 have all come about from short-term factors, and the future for the Japanese vehicle production remains bleak. During 2011, output fell below 9 million for only the second time since the 1970s, owing to natural disasters. Throughout the first half of 2012, Japanese producers were playing catch-up, fulfilling pent-up demand and restocking inventories. They also benefitted from robust domestic demand on the back of government stimulus measures. As a result, total vehicle production rose by 53% year on year during the first half of the year. But as we have moved through H2, this strength has waned. Domestic sales growth has slowed, hindered by an economy that has slipped

back into recession. Overseas demand has also decelerated, particularly since the end of Q3, as Sino-Japanese relations have soured following territorial disputes; total vehicle exports posted declines in annual growth of around 20% in September and October. 2013 offers few prospects for improvement. Domestic demand will remain constrained by weak economic growth, and export demand growth will remain lacklustre. As a result, we forecasts Japanese output to contract by 2.9% next year to 9.8 million vehicles, following growth if 19.8% in 2012. 

Japanese auto industry must overcome major hurdles over the longer-term. A falling population will result in shrinking domestic demand, while a lack of competitiveness will impact export demand. The strength of the yen is increasing the relative cost of assembling vehicles in Japan, threatening to accelerate the process of off-shoring.  For many years Japanese auto makers have been investing heavily in overseas production facilities, so that vehicles can be assembled in locations closer to major demand markets where production costs are lower. We forecast that Japanese vehicle output will contract by an average of 2.3% per annum out to 2030.

## **South Korea** 

South Korea’s auto industry has faltered of late. Solid exports propelled South Korean auto production to a record high of 4.7 million in 2011, up by 9% from 2010, and this trend looked to be continuing through 2012. But exports have slumped during the second half due to weak European demand and domestic labour disruptions. Consequently, total vehicle production is set to contract by 3.7% in 2012. Wood Mackenzie does expect production to bounce back in 2013, thanks to improving export demand, particularly in China, with growth in 2013 of 4.9%. 

As we move into the medium and long term, the challenges facing South Korean vehicle manufacturers are likely to increase. Free-trade agreements with the US and EU will increase competition in the domestic market, while Korean vehicle manufacturers will focus on developing new production capacity overseas, in an attempt to keep operating costs to a minimum and mitigate the risk of currency appreciation. Wood Mackenzie forecasts that Korean vehicle production will peak at 4.8 million units in 2014, and then gradually decline over the remainder of the forecast period. 

### **Total vehicle production in Asia** 



## **China** 

Slow and steady growth has characterised China’s auto market in 2012. Vehicle sales growth has disappointed, as slowing economic growth and poor consumer sentiment have taken their toll. In addition, license plate restrictions in major cities such as Beijing have placed a cap on demand. Through the first 11 months of 2012, total sales grew by just 3.9% from a year earlier. Production has fared slightly better; Chinese carmakers have responded to weak domestic demand, not to mention a fallin

g market share to foreign brands, by exporting increasing volumes to emerging markets. There has been strong growth in exports of low-cost vehicles to places such as Iraq, Russia and Chile – regions not heavily targeted by the major international automakers. As a result, we expect vehicle production to grow by 5.2% in 2012, up from 0.8% in 2011 but still way below the 30%+ rates of 2009-10. Stronger economic growth in 2013, particularly in consumption, should help boost growth next year to 7%. 

Increasing exports mark a new chapter in Chinese vehicle production, which had previously been very much focused on meeting rapidly-growing, domestic demand. While some will no doubt see rising exports as a way to offload excess inventory in a time of poor domestic demand growth, domestic brands such as Geely assert that overseas sales will continue to make up an increasing share of their total sales. In Wood Mackenzie’s view, exports represent a potential upside to our long-term forecast, but we expect that Chinese vehicle production will continue to be determined by domestic demand. The scale of growth opportunities overseas is not as great as it is at home, and competition will be increasingly steep from producers that are assembling vehicles closer to these overseas demand markets. 

Domestic producers will benefit from healthy demand growth in China. As the focus of economic development turns inwards, we expect to see rapid growth in incomes in the interior provinces through the medium and long term. This will make cars increasingly affordable for a larger proportion of the population, fuelling robust growth in vehicle demand and production. However, there is significant uncertainty about the likely level of car ownership in China. Government policy regarding permits and other auto schemes, congestion and elevated fuel prices could all inhibit growth. Wood Mackenzie has relatively conservative expectations around long-term vehicle ownership in China, forecasting the size of the passenger vehicle fleet to increase from 86 million in 2012 to 283 million in 2030. ## **India** 

Like China, India has experienced a sharp slowdown in its auto market since 2010. Production growth fell from 34% in 2010 to 11% in 2011, and is likely to drop further in 2012 to 5.8%. While part of the weakness in auto demand, and thus production, stems from weaker economic growth, it is arguably credit conditions that have really damaged demand. In an attempt to battle high inflation, interest rates were increased significantly in 2010 and 2011, reducing credit availability. This is particularly damaging for Indian auto sales because almost 75% of new cars in India are purchased on finance. 

Although inflation, an

d thus interest rates, will likely come down in 2013, we do not expect to see a sharp acceleration in vehicle sales and production. Economic growth continues to struggle, limiting growth in disposable income. In addition, the Indian government has recently reduced subsidies for diesel (diesel-fuelled cars make up 45% of domestic sales), pushing up the price by 14%, although it remains considerably cheaper than gasoline. Rising fuel prices may impact vehicle demand at the margin, slowing sales growth. Wood Mackenzie forecasts total vehicle output to grow by 6.2% in 2013. 

Beyond the medium term, a rapidly expanding middle class should ensure Indian vehicle demand grows at a robust pace although this will be contingent on a pick-up in infrastructure investment. In order to meet this domestic demand, Wood Mackenzie forecasts Indian vehicle production will expand by 8% per annum on average across the forecast period, one of the world’s fastest growing auto markets. This would take total output in 2030 to 16 million units, roughly two decades after China reached that level, and making it the second-largest vehicle producer globally. 

## **USA** 

The US automotive market has enjoyed a bumper 2012. Through the first ten months of the year, total vehicle sales and production increased by 14% and 22% year on year respectively. By July, vehicle production had reached an annualized rate of 10.9 million vehicles, the fastest since 2007, if still below average output for 2000-2007 of 11.8 million units per year. There are two key factors that have driven growth in US vehicle sales, and hence production. The first is pent-up demand. Between 2008 and 2011 total US sales averaged just fewer than 12 million units per year, compared with 16.7 million in the decade before that. The result of these years of below-trend sales is that the existing vehicle fleet has aged significantly – the average car is now 11 years old. In 2012, US consumers have increasingly been trading in older models for newer, making the most of increased fuel efficiency in a high fuel-cost environment. 

The second factor is credit. Data suggests that the increase in car sales has in part been fuelled by either financing or drawing down savings. In short, consumers spent above their means to meet the pent up demand for cars. A third factor that has benefited production is restocking; inventories fell to extremely low levels in in early 2012 following the supply disruptions of 2012. 

The factors that have resulted in such rapid growth in production in 2012 are not sustainable and as such we expect production growth to slow markedly in 2013 to 1.8%. Inventories have climbed back near to historical norms. The ability of the US consumer to take on more credit is constrained, given that households remain overburdened with debt, and pent-up demand is limited. Future growth in demand will be increasingly determined by income.

### **Vehicles production in the Americas** 



The longer term outlook for production is challenging.  We forecast production to peak in 2015 at 11.2 million units, shy of the 12M level prevalent for much of the past decade despite the fact that US vehicle demand will continue to grow. This is because much new production capacity will be located in Mexico, where assembly costs are lower and many vehicle parts are already produced. 

## **Brazil** 

Brazil’s auto industry has experienced a bounce back in 2h 2012, following a torrid 2011.  Total vehicle production dropped by 7% last year and fell a further 9% year on year through the first half of 2012, as dwindling auto financing schemes and a record-high default rate on auto loans resulted in weak demand. However, in May the government introduced a temporary tax cut on vehicle sales and freed up money in banking system for auto loans, resulting in record sales volumes and a boom in production. We expect this recovery to limit the decline in total production for 2012 to 1.4%. 

The tax incentives are due to expire at the end of 2012, which will limit future demand growth. Nevertheless, we expect to see vehicle output grow by over 6% in in 2013, partially due to the low base effect from 1H 2012, but also owing to improving economic growth. We expect growth to average 3.4% per annum over the duration of the forecast period, relatively slow in comparison to other major emerging economies. This is because Brazil faces a major constraint on vehicle ownership.  Just 10% of the country’s road network is paved, compared with 82% in China, 81% in Russia and 47% in India.  The country will need to deliver on its ambitious infrastructure investment plans if potential vehicle demand is to be realised. 

## **Europe** 

The Eurozone auto market has been a reflection of the wider economy in 2012. Demand has been weak, particularly in the periphery, producers are plagued by excess capacity, and output has contracted once again. Sales across the EU were down by 6.5% year on year through January to October; growth in markets such as the UK and Netherlands has been offset by a 20% contraction in Italian sales and a 32% drop in France. Due to weak economic activity and thus domestic demand, we expect vehicle production across Western Europe to contract by 8.5% in 2012 and by a further 0.3% in 2013. 

Eastern European vehicle production is also suffering from the weakness in demand in the west, which makes up the bulk of demand for production in the region. We expect to see production falls in the Czech Republic, Slovenia, Poland and Turkey in 2012. This is being partially offset by rapid growth in Slovakia, where Kia and Volkswagen are upping production. Overall, Eastern European production will decline by ~1.3% in 2012, but we expect it to bounce back strongly in 2013.
